-- ============================================================================
-- Migration: Add users.last_login_at and backfill from login_events
-- ============================================================================
-- Tables:   users (5M rows), login_events (500M rows, actively growing)
-- Strategy: Add nullable column → pre-aggregate → batched backfill → index
--
-- IMPORTANT COORDINATION:
--   Update your application code FIRST so that all NEW login_events also
--   update users.last_login_at. This migration only backfills history.
--   Without that, logins that occur during the backfill may leave the
--   column slightly out of date.
-- ============================================================================

-- ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
-- 1. ADD COLUMN
-- ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
-- Fast in PG 11+; only a brief metadata lock. No table rewrite because we
-- do NOT add a DEFAULT.
ALTER TABLE users ADD COLUMN IF NOT EXISTS last_login_at timestamptz;


-- ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
-- 2. CREATE SUPPORTING INDEX ON login_events (optional but STRONGLY advised)
-- ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
-- Without an index on (user_id, occurred_at) the MAX() over 500M rows will
-- likely seq-scan and may spill to disk. This also benefits ongoing backfills.
--
-- NOTE: CONCURRENTLY cannot run inside a transaction. If your migration
-- framework wraps migrations in transactions, run this step manually first
-- or use your framework's "disable transaction" option.
-- ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY IF NOT EXISTS idx_login_events_user_id_occurred_at
  ON login_events (user_id, occurred_at DESC);


-- ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
-- 3. BACKFILL: Production-grade (batched, commits between batches)
-- ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
-- Requires PostgreSQL 11+ (procedures with COMMIT).
-- Your migration framework must NOT wrap this in a transaction.
-- If it does, use the single-transaction DO-block fallback below.
-- ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
CREATE OR REPLACE PROCEDURE backfill_users_last_login_at(batch_size int DEFAULT 10000)
LANGUAGE plpgsql
AS $$
DECLARE
    rows_updated int;
BEGIN
    -- Pre-aggregate so we scan the 500M-row table exactly once.
    CREATE TEMP TABLE tmp_last_logins AS
    SELECT user_id, max(occurred_at) AS occurred_at
    FROM login_events
    GROUP BY user_id;

    CREATE INDEX tmp_idx_last_logins ON tmp_last_logins(user_id);
    ANALYZE tmp_last_logins;

    LOOP
        -- Pick a batch of users who still need backfilling AND have logins.
        WITH batch AS (
            SELECT u.id
            FROM users u
            WHERE u.last_login_at IS NULL
              AND EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM tmp_last_logins t WHERE t.user_id = u.id)
            LIMIT batch_size
        )
        UPDATE users u
        SET last_login_at = t.occurred_at
        FROM batch
        JOIN tmp_last_logins t ON t.user_id = batch.id
        WHERE u.id = batch.id;

        GET DIAGNOSTICS rows_updated = ROW_COUNT;
        COMMIT;                       -- release locks, limit WAL growth
        EXIT WHEN rows_updated = 0;
    END LOOP;

    DROP TABLE IF EXISTS tmp_last_logins;
END;
$$;

-- Execute the backfill (adjust batch size if needed)
CALL backfill_users_last_login_at(10000);

-- Clean up the helper procedure
DROP PROCEDURE IF EXISTS backfill_users_last_login_at;

-- 3-alt. BACKFILL: Single-transaction fallback (PG < 11 or strict frameworks)

3. **Monitor disk I/O and replication lag** during the backfill. With 500M rows, the initial `GROUP BY` may take several minutes and use significant temporary disk space if `work_mem` is low.
